subtopic: NATO-REPORT BY MINISTER UPON RETURN FROM PARIS MEETING

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: NATO-REPORT BY MINISTER UPON RETURN FROM PARIS MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like with the consent of the house, and in accordance with regular practice, to report briefly on the NATO ministerial meeting in Paris from which the Minister of National Defence and I have just returned.
The major problems which arose at the last meeting in Brussels concerned the process of adjusting to the consequences of France's decision to withdraw from NATO's integrated military structure. By contrast, at this meeting, France's relationship with the alliance was not a subject of discussion, since the necessary adjustments had already been largely completed. Our discussions reflected the fact that a new relationship between France and the 14 other nations in the alliance is being achieved.
The new foreign minister of Germany, Mr. Brandt, made an important statement. The coalition government having just taken office in Germany, particular interest was attached to this first statement of policy. Mr. Brandt gave welcome assurance of the German government's dedication to the alliance and of its desire to make progress in its relations with the countries of eastern Europe.
Mr. Brandt also spoke of his government's intention to promote contacts between the peoples of west Germany and east Germany, without compromising the Federal Republic's position on the non-recognition of the German Democratic Republic or on the important goal of German reunification. He stressed the German government's intention to maintain democratic institutions. He reiterated that the Federal Republic seeks neither national control of atomic weapons nor national ownership of such weapons.
In December, 1964, Canada proposed a study of the future of the alliance. This suggestion was adopted by the council but was not acted upon, for fear that it would lead to a break with France At this meeting,
however, with France already having taken its action in respect of NATO, it was decided at the suggestion of the Belgian foreign minister that the time was now ripe for a wide-ranging study of the objectives and future tasks of the alliance. This study, which is to be presented to the meeting in December, 1967, could enlarge the area for political activity by the alliance.
The main attention at this meeting was directed to east-west relations. A full study prepared after the Brussels meeting confirmed that it was desirable to improve our relations with the countries of eastern Europe, bearing in mind that the over-all objective is a peaceful settlement in Europe. The meeting recognized that for the present bilateral relations represented the most likely area for immediate progress.
As one suggestion for improving east-west relations, a number of countries, including Canada, alluded to the possibility-and I do not suggest that this is for the immediate future-of reciprocal reductions in opposing NATO and Warsaw pact forces.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
In the political sphere, the Russians have recently shown interest in encouraging improved relations between east and west. This is an attitude which NATO's military strength has encouraged over the years s nee NATO was formed. However, Soviet forces in eastern Europe are being continually strengthened. Accordingly, while we want to encourage improved east-west relations, we cannot afford to reduce our over-all level of forces unless the Soviet side is prepared to do likewise.
I suggested that it might be useful to keep under review possibilities for gradual reductions in western and Soviet forces in central Europe. Then if opportunities arise we should know what was reasonable to propose on our side, and what reciprocal action we might expect on the other side.
For Canada's part, we continue to support the alliance as the best guarantee of the security of its members. We consider that Canada's interests and responsibilities require at present an appropriate continuing contribution to the military strength of NATO.
NATO, of course, has great military strength. This strength is contributed by the
11282	COMMONS
Report by Minister of Paris Meeting members of the alliance collectively and its management is equally a collective responsibility. Important progress was made at the meeting with the establishment of new improved machinery for nuclear defence management. Membership in the new organization does not increase or affect the nuclear commitments of its members. Its purpose is to permit fuller and wider participation in the formulation of NATO's nuclear defence policy and to give the non-nuclear countries a readier appreciation of what is involved in planning for defence against possible nuclear attack.
Another important aspect of this decision is its direct connection with the practical pursuit of disarmament. We are determined that this new method of co-operative defence will make it unnecessary for the western countries to set up any new joint nuclear force such as the proposed multilateral force. Indeed, I believe that what we are doing in NATO is already helping in bringing within reach a non-proliferation agreement, that is, an agreement to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons.
With this statement, Mr. Speaker, I would like to table copies in English and French of the final communique.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: NATO-REPORT BY MINISTER UPON RETURN FROM PARIS MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that the minister is to be congratulated on the report that he has given. It is terse and reasonably complete. It indicates that the meeting of the NATO powers did bring about a new stance, if one can use that expression.
Mr. Willy Brandt brought to NATO new concepts which cannot but be beneficial. In particular I refer to the agreement set out in the communique whereby these nations, all of them that are members of NATO, agreed that there should be a call for development of human, economic and cultural contacts between the two parts of Germany. This is a long step forward from the occurrences of the last 15 years.
In so far as reduction of forces is concerned, Britain today has some 55,000 members of its armed services stationed on the continent; the United States has 225,000 and Canada has the force that it has had there in recent years. At this time, when there seems to be a diminution in the tensions between east and west, there are widespread demands that there should be a pronounced reduction in those forces. The demands spring from the point of view of the assurance of peace, and also to benefit the economic situation in the various

DEBATES	December 19, 1966
countries, because the contribution to the NATO forces has added greatly to the costs of those countries.
I am beginning to feel that with a diminution of tension, and because there is a preponderance of nuclear power in the United States the ground forces do not have the importance they had from the beginning of NATO.
Canada should give consideration to reducing the numbers of her forces on the continent of Europe. There was reference to the contribution by Canada to non-proliferation of nuclear weapons. I am not going to bring back other days, sir, but in 1963 when we took that stand, realizing that the day of the bomber was over, we were strongly criticized by the Liberal party. In the intervening period they have become converted to the idea that there should not be proliferation. This is indeed worthy of comment and appreciation.
I should have liked to hear the minister place before this house the reaction of the nuclear powers to the Canadian government's adoption of unification of the forces. That would have been an interesting story. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) shakes his head in an affirmative way. We have seen him do that before when the facts were opposite. I should like to hear him in this regard, because I am sure he rose to heights of eloquence in placing before the NATO powers the fact that Canada is going to become a pioneer in the field of removing all the insignia and traditions of the past.
I wish the Minister of National Defence would translate that nod to a vocal assertion. I am sure the house would find it interesting because the information the press gave is that the nations of NATO laughed at the idea. We shall see if we are able to get an answer from the Minister of National Defence, something we have not succeeded in doing up to the present time.
However, if the Secretary of State for External Affairs always reports to parliament with the lucidity and clarity he exhibited today, he will always receive a welcome.

subtopic: NATO-REPORT BY MINISTER UPON RETURN FROM PARIS MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) has said so many kind and flattering words to the minister that I will not endeavour to repeat them.
We shall read very carefully and with a great deal of interest the statement of the minister and the communique. May I say, however, that I believe we and many other
December 19, 1966
Canadians may have very serious doubt and regret about the fact that Canada has felt it necessary to take part in a committee to examine or to concern itself with the exercise of the nuclear component of the alliance. We believe it would be better for Canada to take the position that we are not a nuclear power and do not wish to have any responsibility in any shape or form for this nuclear strategy. Also, along with many other people in the world, we view with apprehension any suggestion that West Germany in any shape or form should have any control, or participation in the control of nuclear weapons.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
We believe this has been one of the obstacles to a non-proliferation treaty. We would much prefer Canada's taking the position that she has no wish to participate in the nuclear strategy. We should say to our ally, West Germany, that we think it would be better for the peace of the world if it, too, took no part whatsoever, not only in the actual physical control of nuclear weapons, but in any nuclear strategy, and as a member of the NATO alliance renounced any wish to take any such part in any way, shape or form.
I regret that in this statement once again there was absolutely nothing definite about any proposal made by Canada to phase out or get out of the present tactical nuclear role in which she is engaged in Europe. We believe that the diminution of tension to which the minister referred provided a first rate opportunity for Canada to say that her contribution to the alliance should be purely in the form of a mobile force without nuclear armaments of any k nd whatsoever. We regret that we are apparently failing to do this, and that the m nister has said absolutely nothing about acquainting our allies with an intention, not to reduce our forces as the Leader of the Opposition suggests but to opt out altogether from this nuclear role. These omissions we think are serious and important, and we hope we will have a chance to hear something from the minister in respect of these matters.

subtopic: NATO-REPORT BY MINISTER UPON RETURN FROM PARIS MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my comments will be brief on welcoming back the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of National Defence (Messrs. Martin and Hellyer) who have just returned from the last NATO meeting held in France.
According to the statement made by the minister, it would seem that recent political events in Germany had caused some concern
Report by Minister of Paris Meeting to the other members of NATO. However, the fact that reunification was studied should lead us to believe that Europe is committing itself to finding a way which will bring peace to that area.
One point worries me however, and I wonder if I understood clearly the statement made by the minister, which statement I am anxious to read at my leisure. I note that once again we discussed disarmament while unfortunately, taking care to ensure that we are armed to the teeth. We are told that the United States will soon conduct another nuclear explosion; in fact, some are being announced here and there throughout the world. New countries are adopting nuclear arms, taking great care to say that these are intended for defence. But the fact remains that nuclear arms are dangerous to handle. I feel that no effort should be spared toward disarmament and that, once and for all, that aspect of peace should be looked into. So long as we plan for war, we cannot achieve peace.
We will study the statement made by the minister on the NATO meeting in order to benefit therefrom as much as possible.

subtopic: NATO-REPORT BY MINISTER UPON RETURN FROM PARIS MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we welcome the report of the Secretary of State for External Affairs following his visit to the NATO ministerial conference. I would have appreciated some reference by the minister to reports which appear in today's press regarding the withdrawal of some of the R.C.A.F. squadrons, both reconnaissance and attack, serving at the present time under NATO. Likewise it would have been appreciated had the minister told us something about the relocation of No. 1 wing at Marville, and the headquarters at Metz. While this was not a direct concern it must have formed part of the discussions which were held, because it is related to our own NATO contribution.
It is reassuring to hear the minister suggest that the policy of the government is to continue its support in the NATO alliance. I think it is realized that while the United Nations has its place in the whole area of peaceful negotiation in the world, the real peace keeping organization is NATO, and the fact that Canada will continue her role in that organization is most important. I had hoped the minister might have mentioned the decision that will have to be made regarding the approximately 70,000 troops that France has in Germany at the present time, and whether

Report of Mediator in Railway Dispute these forces will continue under some bilateral agreement.
It was reassuring also to hear the minister say that the new German foreign minister and the defence minister reiterate the stand taken by their predecessors, that Germany really has no intention of wanting any part in or control of the NATO nuclear deterrent. This does not detract from the fact that it is now general knowledge that the communist buildup of their forces on the eastern side of the dividing line in Europe is continuing to increase.
Unless there can be some agreement that gives the assurance that this will not continue, and that there will be a co-operative decrease in the forces of the Warsaw pact countries, we cannot really talk about cutting down our own contribution. Co-operative defence is one of the reassuring areas of co-operation among nations, such as we have among the nations of the NATO alliance.

subtopic: PRUDENTIAL FINANCE CORPORATION-OBSERVATIONS OF MINISTER FOLLOWING STATEMENT OF WILLIAM GRUBER

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PRUDENTIAL FINANCE CORPORATION-OBSERVATIONS OF MINISTER FOLLOWING STATEMENT OF WILLIAM GRUBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the questions which were directed to me last week, and of certain
December 19, 1966

statements made by Mr. William Gruber over the week end, I thought I might make a brief statement.
First, may I say that Mr. William Gruber was once employed by Mr. Morris Stein, the former auditor of the Prudential Finance Corporation, and was dismissed by Mr. Stein. Mr. Gruber first contacted the Toronto office of the Superintendent of Insurance in January of 1966. Because the department of insurance had no legal authority to assure him that he would be protected from legal action, he refused to disclose even the name of the company about which he said he had information. From the remarks which Mr. Gruber made, however, officials of the department of insurance concluded that he was probably referring to Prudential Finance.
As I said, he did not say that; this was just an inference which the officials drew. The [DOT]department of insurance was already exercising close surveillance over its federally incorporated subsidiary, The North American General Insurance Company, as a result of its recent purchase by the Prudential group. The result of this surveillance was in part the discovery in November of the theft of securities from the North American General Insurance Company.
Subsequent to his discussions with the department of insurance in January, Mr. Gruber met with an official of the Department of National Revenue and, under the protection of the Income Tax Act, made certain statements about Prudential Finance. He was informed that the Income Tax Act prevented that department from forwarding that information to any other department or authority.

subtopic: PRUDENTIAL FINANCE CORPORATION-OBSERVATIONS OF MINISTER FOLLOWING STATEMENT OF WILLIAM GRUBER
speechtext: Can the minister inform us of the date?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PRUDENTIAL FINANCE CORPORATION-OBSERVATIONS OF MINISTER FOLLOWING STATEMENT OF WILLIAM GRUBER
speechtext:
I do not know the exact date but it was some time in January. As I said, Mr. Gruber was informed by the officials at that time that the Income Tax Act prevented that department from forwarding information to any other department or authority.
When the department of insurance inquired further from the Department of National Revenue, that department properly refused to divulge any information, but did say that there was nothing in what Mr. Gruber said that was of concern to the department of insurance, nor did his statements contain any evidence of tax evasion. The officials of the Department of National Revenue also indicated that they had had previous contacts with Mr. Gruber on a number of occasions, which
Bankruptcy
had led them to feel that he was generally an unreliable informant.
The department of insurance has had no correspondence whatsoever with Mr. Gruber on the subject of Prudential Finance or the North American General Insurance Company. The only correspondence it has had with him at all referred to a toy company, which is not related. This letter was forwarded to the Superintendent of Bankruptcy by the department of insurance. The acknowledgement received in reply by Mr. Gruber is apparently being displayed by him as proof that he told these agencies about the affairs of Prudential. It is not related.
Neither I nor any other minister has ever met Mr. Gruber personally. In fact his first direct approach to any minister was on December 13, 1966, just a week ago, when Mr. Gruber left a telephone message at my office indicating that he intended to make public what he called "the facts" about Prudential at a creditors meeting on December 15.
He indicated that the Ontario Securities Commission knew of this matter, and he also gave the name of Inspector Thurston of the Ontario Police Commission as a further reference. He said as well that he had corresponded with the hon. member for Yukon, Mr. Erik Nielsen.
When Mr. Gruber spoke with officials of the department of insurance in January he refused to provide them with anything that they could possibly refer either to another federal department or to the authorities of the province of Ontario. In any case he made it clear that he himself was contacting other federal government departments and the Ontario authorities with the intention of revealing the information he had refused to the Superintendent of Insurance. I understand that Mr. Gruber now denies this, but this was the clear understanding of federal officials.
Officials of the federal department of insurance have a close and continuing contact with officials of the Ontario department of insurance. In fact over the past year federal and provincial insurance officials have had numerous conversations involving North American General Insurance, Wenworth Insurance, which are subsidiaries of Prudential Finance, in the course of their regular business.
Federal officials have been aware for some time of the Ontario government's interest in Prudential Finance. Had Mr. Gruber provided any worth-while additional information, it would have been transmitted to them in the normal way. He did not do so.

December 19, 1966
Bankruptcy
The office of the federal Superintendent of Bankruptcy was not contacted at all by Mr. Gruber about Prudential Finance or its related companies until after Prudential had made a proposal to its creditors in November of 1966. The Superintendent of Bankruptcy had no previous knowledge of the affairs of Prudential Finance, and in any case his responsibility commences when a firm is declared bankrupt or makes a proposal to its creditors, and not before.
However, I am informed by the office of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy which received last week this information from Mr. Morris Stein, the former auditor of the Prudential Finance Corporation of Toronto, that Mr. Ted Brown, chief auditor for the Ontario Securities Commission, has met with Mr. Stein, to discuss the affairs of Prudential on several occasions since 1963. In March of this year there was an inquiry into the affairs of Prudential Finance at which Mr. Harry Bray, director, Ontario Securities Commission, Mr. Ted Brown, Ontario Securities Commission, Mr. G. Gillman, Ontario Securities Commission, Mr. Brien, president, Prudential Finance, Mr. William Deslauriers, of Tory, Tory, Des-lauriers and Binnington, Mr. Morris Stein and a stenographer were present.
In June of this year Mr. Gillman of the Ontario securities commission reviewed the affairs of Prudential with Mr. Stein once again.
Prudential Finance is a provincially chartered company and the Ontario authorities have been aware of its problems for some time. The federal government is concerned when any group of Canadians suffers in this way. We have a particular interest in this latest case, beyond the general protection of Canadian investors, because a federal company, North American General Insurance, was undermined by the collapse of a provincial company-Prudential Finance. The collapse of Prudential Finance and others that have gone before could only have been prevented by the improvement of provincial laws and administration.
Our jurisdiction is limited; nevertheless we are not satisfied with the general level of protection afforded the investor in Canada. The provincial authorities must find ways to make that protection more adequate, and the federal government is prepared to assist them. We are already reviewing our own laws and administration as they relate to federally incorporated finance companies. We urge the

provinces to do the same within their areas of jurisdiction.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
In conclusion, may I make clear, in view of what Mr. Gruber said over the week end, that I have never been contacted personally by Mr. Gruber at any time and he did not call my office until after the collapse of Prudential on December 13. At no time did he reveal to the department of insurance anything of value, not even the name of the company.
The Ontario authorities were fully aware of the Prudential Finance, which is a provincially incorporated company subject to provincial laws and administration.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PRUDENTIAL FINANCE CORPORATION-OBSERVATIONS OF MINISTER FOLLOWING STATEMENT OF WILLIAM GRUBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just listened to the minister producing a mystery within a mystery. He obviously had a prepared statement designed in general to exculpate the government of Canada and, in particular, himself. With the greatest respect to the minister, and accepting his statement that the man in question never communicated with him, that in no way answers the situation that has been created.
It is the most amazing story that the minister tells. Gruber did meet with government officials in Toronto and no one knew what he was talking about. The officials had a suspicion he was talking about the Prudential Finance Corporation, and when they were informed of that they made certain investigations, apparently, although they did not say anything to the government of the province of Ontario.
The minister says now that the government of Canada is disturbed over the losses. Why was there no communication? The excuse he gives is that the Department of National Revenue could not furnish any information because of the provision of the statute. If ever there was an example of transparent excuse and subterfuge, that is one. While this department plays around and the minister engages in this artful dodging, 20,000 Canadians will have their insurance policies cancelled, according to the liquidator. The minister produces an alibi for the fact nothing was done to notify the government of Ontario.

I feel sorry for the minister. There he was in solitary isolation, nobody telling him what was going on. At the same time there apparently was information of such a nature that the informant was afraid unless he was given protection, he would be in danger. What he was afraid of I do not know, but that is what he said. Surely a person with information he was afraid to reveal in detail should have produced a very complete and thorough investigation. It is a mysterious story. It is patent, Mr. Speaker, that the minister today is trying to get away from the responsibility of the federal government.

They have no responsibility. That has been their attitude on bankruptcies for too long. That has been their attitude. They say: We have no responsibility. Surely this government cannot stand idly by in a matter coming under a federal charter. Surely a simple inquiry by the Superintendent of Insurance is not enough in a case involving dislocation and financial manipulations on a
Bankruptcy
massive scale. Yet the minister's whole attitude is that there is really nothing for the Government of Canada to be concerned about.
Are we to tolerate piratical actions by those who operate insurance companies? What happened to the $500,000 in securities? They were there in September and gone in November. The minister says nothing can be done. Surely some law should be in effect regarding foreign corporations in Canada.

subtopic: PRUDENTIAL FINANCE CORPORATION-OBSERVATIONS OF MINISTER FOLLOWING STATEMENT OF WILLIAM GRUBER
speechtext: Why did not the right hon. gentleman bring one in?

subtopic: PRUDENTIAL FINANCE CORPORATION-OBSERVATIONS OF MINISTER FOLLOWING STATEMENT OF WILLIAM GRUBER
speechtext:
Surely the federal government, which more than any other government is responsible for the direction of economic development is responsible to Canadians who invest in companies, as these did. Something must be done other than wafting idle verbiage before the House of Commons, and believing the matter has been settled.
Surely, when the national economy and the savings of so many are involved, there is need for more than a passing gesture representing almost contemptuous disregard of people's rights. The overwhelming number of businessmen and industrialists in Canada are honest and progressive; they operate on a fair and reasonable basis.

Sir, because of the revelation Canada's reputation for honesty and integrity in business is being challenged in various parts of the world. We cannot permit Canada to be a happy hunting ground for unscrupulous operators who believe that the law of the jungle should be their guiding theme.

I will have more to say about this on a later occasion. What the minister has done today is to open a box so that we just get a glimpse of what it contains. The degree of supervision exercised over the activities of companies under federal responsibility is not what it should be. There have been several instances of sufficient magnitude in the past two years to cause uneasiness and disquiet. Before I conclude, I have certain questions I should like to address to the minister. Did the federal government or the office of the bankruptcy division receive information from Mr. Gruber regarding no fewer than five other bankruptcies this year? Let them shake themselves out of this lethargy, so that in the future not only other Canadians may be protected from wrongdoing, but so that those people who invested because this was a company under federal responsibility will not be made the goats, and suffer, because they believed that an insurance company was something apart from the ordinary run of corporations. They thought that when they took out insurance they would be protected, and that when they bought shares in an insurance company they could do so in the confidence, on the basis of experience and law, that examinations would be made regularly to the end that they would not suffer financial loss.

The minister laughs and smiles. He and his hon. friends smile while unfortunate people are suffering losses.

In January of this year, Mr. Gruber said he had information to disclose which would be significant to anyone concerned about the affairs of Prudential Finance or its subsidiaries-
The minister went on to say that Mr. Gruber would only make the disclosure if he were offered legal protection. To date I have not heard what sort of legal protection he was asking. The main point in that statement is that he said he had information which would concern anyone interested in the affairs of Prudential Finance or its subsidiaries. subtopic: PRUDENTIAL FINANCE CORPORATION-OBSERVATIONS OF MINISTER FOLLOWING STATEMENT OF WILLIAM GRUBER
speechtext:
May I ask the minister to stop being defensive, and to cease concerning himself about who surmised what? The important fact, as far as the Canadian people are concerned, is that the officials of his department had reason to be concerned about a company, a subsidiary of Prudential Finance, over which the federal government had jurisdiction, and it was their duty to do something about it. It was also their duty at that time to get in touch with the provincial authorities. It was not good enough for them to take the lofty position the minister took on Friday, as appears at page 11271, that as far as he knew Mr. Gruber passed the information along to the provincial authorities at the same time as he passed it to the federal government. Mr. Gruber now denies having done that. I do not think any member of this house is concerned with precisely how much reliance is to be placed on Mr. Gruber's statement. I have never met him in my life; never spoken to him. I submit that what is of concern to this parliament, and what the minister would do well to admit for the sake of Canada, is that there was a slip up-there was a failure to act when the department should have acted last January.
If the minister had the touch of greatness which is required, I believe he would do this. It is not his personal responsibility, and we would know that having admitted a failure in this case a s'milar failure was less likely to occur in the future. But one cannot help being concerned at this attempt, now, to gloss over something which is indefensible, this failure on the part of officials of the hon. gentleman's department who might otherwise be entirely competent and good officials-I do not know them, either. But in this case they did a disservice to Canada and a disservice to the policyholders and investors who had trusted Prudential Finance and North American General Insurance.
I want to make two or three points of a more positive character. It seems to me this entire, regrettable and shocking case shows that there is great danger in permitting any
Bankruptcy
person, and any group of people who are concerned with nothing else but the profit they can make out of it, to set up finance companies, to lend poor consumers' money at exorbitant interest rates, and then to permit them to proliferate into all sorts of subsidiaries which may swallow up insurance companies at the expense of the policyholders and of the integrity of this country.
I say that what is needed is not an inquiry by a parliamentary committee, which seems to me to be very limited indeed. On our behalf, I urge the minister to consult with the provincial authorities in this country, to make a thorough inquiry in this entire field, both federal and provincial, of these small insurance companies and of these, as it turns out, thieving finance and acceptance corporations.
I say secondly, Mr. Speaker, this situation clearly shows a lack of adequate legislation on the federal level and the provincial level. It is not enough for the minister to blame the Ontario government and to try to clear his skirts by doing that. I agree with the minister that the Ontario authorities are fully as much responsible, if perhaps not even more directly responsible, as the federal authorities. But it seems to me the federal government has a responsibility to convene a conference of all provincial authorities, not only the insurance companies but the authorities within the provinces, in order that a combined and consistent effort can be made to plug the loopholes in our legislation and a stop called to th:s thieving that has gone on, with the failures that have followed.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, as we approach our centenary, may I say it is a heartbreaking thing to see these important events, affecting the lives and the future of thousands of Canadians, taking place in separate compartments in this country. The lack of co-operation between Ottawa and Queen's Park, and the similar lack of co-operation between Ottawa and other provincial centres, is a disservice to this country. I express the hope that th s sad incident, which cannot now be cured so far as the investors, the policy holders and the many people who have lost their savings are concerned, will teach us to establish a line of authority and co-operation between the federal and provincial governments that will be of real value to our country.
On behalf of our party I should like to urge the right hon. Prime Minister that the federal government seek to co-operate with the provincial government of Ontario, and other governments if they are involved, to find some

December 19, 1966
Bankruptcy
way of compensating the poor investors and policy holders who have suffered from this tragedy which our government and the provincial government failed to prevent.

subtopic: PRUDENTIAL FINANCE CORPORATION-OBSERVATIONS OF MINISTER FOLLOWING STATEMENT OF WILLIAM GRUBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to try to attach any blame, or to comment on the relationships of the failure of the Prudential Finance Corporation to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp). However, I think the minister has a responsibility to see whether or not there are any other federally chartered insurance companies that may be controlled by these so-called "10 percenter'' finance companies. These finance companies, of course, are under the jurisdiction of provincial governments.
I agree that we have had too many of these failures which have involved the savings of a lot of innocent people. Therefore, there is an important responsibility on the part of the Minister of Finance to see that these insurance companies are not being bought up or controlled by this type of finance company.
The minister said earlier that there was nothing said to the officers in his department that was worthy of referring to any other department or, for that matter, to the officers in the government of Ontario. When Mr. Gruber came to the office of the superintendent of insurance and explained to the officials there that there were some problems involved, I cannot accept the fact that those officers did not at once examine the corporate structure of the company to see how it was controlled. Surely if there is any reason at all for requiring a federal charter for insurance companies, it must be to give some legal protection to the people who invest in those companies.
I am not suggesting that a federal charter in any way guarantees success within those companies, but it certainly ought to guarantee honesty, something which has not been present so far as the administration of the North American General Insurance Company is concerned.
The minister also said that Mr. Gruber never called at his office, never telephoned him, and so on. That is of no particular consequence to me because I think there are other ways of communicating information, such as to the department, and the department should act on that information. The minister went on to say that he is not satisfied with the federal legislation we have at the moment respecting this kind of problem, and that he is not satisfied with the federal legislation we have at the moment respecting this kind of problem, and that he is not satisfied with what is in

the provincial statutes. We, too, are not satisfied in that respect, and we can at least agree with him that something ought to be done to tighten up these laws so that there may not be a repetition of this incident.
We would support the suggestion that an inquiry should be made into this matter. I am not entirely sure a parliamentary committee should be the first step taken to look into the matter, but I think it might be a logical second step, after we have had a thorough investigation by a royal commission to make sure there are no more corporate structures of this kind whereby provincially chartered companies have control of federally chartered insurance companies.
If there are such corporate structures and we see that there may be the possibility, or the probability, of some of them being in a weak financial condition with respect to their obligations, then some action should be taken, and taken right away. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say on behalf of this party that we are not satisfied with the explanation that has been given today or with what was done with the information that was in the hands of some of the federal government officials several months ago. We hope we are not going to have any more excuses or buck-passing in the house, and that positive action will be taken to clear away this mess and strengthen legislation so that there will be no repetition of it.

subtopic: CALENDAR REFORM
CALENDAR REFORM
speechtext:
1.	Has any consideration been given by the government to the subject of calendar reform?
2.	If so, when and by what agency of government?
3.	Have any tentative conclusions been achieved?
4.	Have there been any negotiations or discussions with any international organizations or with other nations on the subject of calendar reform?
5.	If so, what is the nature and result of such negotiations or discussions?

speakeroldname: Mr. John R. Matheson (Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: CALENDAR REFORM
speechtext:
1. The subject of calendar reform was considered in 1955 by several departments concerned with the effects of a reform of the calendar as a result of a request by the Secretary-General of the United Nations that the Canadian government forward its views on the desirability of reforming the calendar.
2.	See answer to previous question. The matter was considered in 1955 by an interdepartmental committee on calendar reform composed of representatives of the Departments of Citizenship and Immigration, External Affairs, Labour, Mines and Technical Surveys (Dominion Observatories), Secretary of State, Trade and Commerce (Dominion Bureau of Statistics) and Transport.
3.	No Arm conclusions have been reached on this matter. The reply to the Secretary-General's request, embodying the recommendations of the interdepartmental committee, stated that "the Canadian Government has come to the conclusion that a study, under the auspices of the Economic and Social Council, of the possibilities of calendar reform might prove useful. While expressing an interest in a study of calendar reform proposals and possibilities, the Canadian government does not wish at this time to support or commit itself to any specific reform". Generally speaking, it is considered that for Canada to initiate a reform of the calendar on its own would be to invite many inconveniences, not only to ourselves, but to other countries dealing with us. Consequently, whatever reforms are made should be made on an international basis. Should a serious international interest in reform plans develop, the government would be prepared to consider the question in a worldwide context under the auspices of the United Nations.
4.	The question of world calendar reform was considered in 1956 by the twenty-first session of the United Nations Economic and Social Council, of which Canada was a member at that time. In the brief debate which
Questions
took place in ECOSOC most representatives expressed the view that the time was not ripe calendar reform. At the close of the discussion a proposal to adjourn indefinitely consideration of the question was adopted by a vote of 15 to 0 with three abstentions. Canada abstained on this proposal because we were unwilling to vote in favour of the indefinite postponement of this question and felt that continued study of calendar reform under United Nations auspices would be worthwhile. At the same time, we recognized that there was relatively little interest internationally in this question. There has been no further discussion on the matter of calendar reform in the United Nations since 1956.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question which I should like to direct to the Prime Minister. It deals with the fact that on April 30, 1965 I asked this following question of the Minister of Finance:
Will the minister tell the house if the government intends to take any action on the Porter Commission recommendation concerning securities administration and control?
The answer given by the minister at that time, Hon. Walter L. Gordon, was that the matter was under study and had been for some time. In view of the circumstances of this past week, would the Prime Minister now give very urgent consideration to carrying out the recommendation of the Porter Commission dealing with the national securities commission, in co-operation with the provincial securities commissions, and also in co-operation with the S.E.C. in the United States.

speakeroldname: Righi Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: FINANCE
subsubtopic: ACTION ON ROYAL COMMISSION RECOMMENDATION RESPECTING SECURITIES CONTROL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend knows the federal government has been looking into this matter since the day of that question, indeed,
December 19, 1968

before that. We set up a task force under a very competent and experienced lawyer who visited every provincial capital and discussed the problem with all the provincial governments. As a result of that discussion and the report which he made to the federal government, a federal-provincial conference was held which reached certain conclusions. It is hoped that these conclusions will result in legislative action, both federally and provincially, in order to deal with this very serious problem in a more efficient way in the future than perhaps has been possible in the past. As has been pointed out, action already has been taken at both levels of government and we hope before long to be in a position to announce what we will be able to do legislatively. Order, please. When the committee rose on Friday, December 16, an amendment to clause 3 proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was under consideration. The amendment reads as follows:
That clause 3 of Bill C-251 be amended by deleting from sub-section (1) of the new section 8 being enacted thereby, the words "minus one dollar for each two full dollars of his monthly base income, being one-twelfth of his income for the preceding year", as found in lines 1, 2, and 3 on page 3 of the bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a few words to say about the amendment. First of all, I should like to say that there is a growing tendency in the government for interdepartmental snooping. When I first came to the
11306	COMMONS
Old Age Security Act Amendment house it was a recognized fact, as I understood it, that no one was permitted to look into the returns of the Department of National Revenue.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
No information was given out. Next, we had the social security number, and the suspicion grew that this was the opening of the door for snooping. Then, along came the Canada Pension Plan Act and the suspicion grew that it was necessary to have interdepartmental communication, it became a fact. Now, the government has gone a step farther. There must be communication between the officials administering old age security, or the guaranteed income, and the Department of National Revenue. If this trend continues, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare has to agree with it, we shall become completely state controlled in the too distant future. There will be no private life, everybody's business will be public knowledge. This, I say, is a downward path and is certainly invading privacy as it has never been invaded before.
Another thing bothering me, and this was brought out by the Minister of Transport, is that the old people will be paid 2 per cent extra for the rising cost of living per year or $1.50 per year. That is completely wrong on principle because everybody knows that food costs last year went up by 10 per cent and rents by 10 to 20 per cent. Giving them only 2 per cent or $1.50 is a disgraceful way to use our older people.
It means, Mr. Chairman, that in 1975 that 2 per cent base will remain the same over the year. One only has to think back to 1935 and compare the dollar of that day with the dollar of today to realize that that dollar only has one third of the value of the 1966 dollar. I am sure that can be verified by asking the Minister of Public Works who sat in the government at that time, I believe as secretary to the minister of trade and commerce. In one year alone, recently, inflation increased by 15 per cent. How, in all sincerity, can we ask the old people to accept 2 per cent, when many of them cannot work to help themselves. If they do work, they will be penalized. The minister will not grant them any benefit even though they earn low wages.

Notwithstanding any other act or law, no officer or employee of Her Majesty shall be required, in connection with any legal proceedings, to give evidence relating to any information that is privileged under subsection (1) -
Now, what is the situation that we find here? We find that the minister is asking parliament to enact that in the courts of the land-and it is in the courts that the rights and obligations of citizens should be determined-no officer or employee shall give a breath of information, notwithstanding anything in any other act. In other words it will not be right to demand of the public service that they disclose information; that is the principle asserted here. And this is the same minister who in respect of the preceding proposed subsection, said that public servants within the government may pass confidential information back and forth between one another, at will, it order that privately, behind closed doors, they may determine the rights and obligations of citizens.
That is the situation. How can the minister, who says in respect of proposed subsection 3 that this confidential information can be passed back and forth behind the backs of the people, then say in respect of the next subsection that with regard to legal proceedings in Her Majesty's courts of Canada-in which courts by our tradition the rights and obligations of our citizens are determined-this information which they are so ready and so willing to make available to everyone for purposes of private snooping, cannot be produced?

I should like to put a direct question to the minister in connection with the administration of the act. Let us suppose that the income of an applicant is questioned. Let us suppose that the spouse of an applicant has given information concerning her income. Let us also suppose that the applicant and the spouse dispute the information which is in the possession of the investigating officer. In such a case, I would assume, the officer interviewing the applicant would say: "You say you only got $300 last year, but your employer says you got $500." The applicant says: "That is not true; I do not believe what you are telling me."
Is it not to be expected that at this point the applicant would go to his wife's employer and say: "I got this information from the man at the national health and welfare office. He has your income tax returns and he say that you paid more than I said."

I got this from an investigating officer of the Department of National Health and Welfare, and he has the information on his file"? It seems to me there is both a legal and practical implication here, and I cannot think of anything worse respecting the confidentiality of income tax returns. This is a practical example of what could happen.
The broadness of the words proposed, "relating to any applicant, beneficiary or spouse" could extend the provision into other

I am sure there would be no point in saying that the information will be revealed only to somebody in Ottawa, because the information will be passed to the local investigating officer, in Vancouver, Parry Sound, or anywhere else, who will be dealing with the individual applicant. Despite what the minister may intend, there is a loophole in the proposed section as it now reads, which might be taken advantage of by someone. Our purpose is to put the bill in such a form that it will not have to be modified within 12 months, and that it will not permit people to take advantage of some omission on our part. The suggestion made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni might well meet the objections that have been raised from other quarters in the chamber.

As I understand the minister, all he wants to know is whether an applicant is giving correct information with regard to his income. If we are correct in our assumption that a very small percentage of people will give inaccurate information, perhaps a few deliberately and some by inadvertence or error, then why open up the Income Tax Act and the secrecy surrounding returns? The point I wish to make is that by suggesting the sampling of a certain number of applications the minister is opening the way for a game of Russian roullette with the problems of our old people. It seems to me that the danger in respect of these proposed sections is that they open the way for spiteful letters to be written by people who do not sign their names. These letters might be written to a department indicating that some old age pensioner is not entitled to receive the supplementary benefit. I think by this action the minister is opening up a Pandora's box of every type of imaginable evil. I hope he will consider the very good suggestion made here in respect of amendments to proposed section 17 which were presented by those who have taken part in this debate.
I seem to recall an occasion, under the former administration, when a court held that an income tax return was compellable evidence and the Minister of National Revenue of that day immediately caused an amendment to be made to the law to see that the complete umbrella of privilege was given to the income tax return. I commend that course to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I should like also to point out that if these 500 people who are hired full time to look into these returns wish to keep themselves occupied, surely they are going to have to write to an equivalent number of civil servants in the Department of National Revenue who will haul out these returns and give the answers. Not only will we have the direct proliferation of 500 full time civil servants plus the part time civil servants in the Department of National Health and Welfare-what an empire builder the minister could become-but in the Department of National Revenue, not for empire building but for the sake of preserving the department's sanity, hundreds of civil servants would have to be hired to answer these questions.
It is easier to ask these questions than it is to answer them, so the net result may be that for every new employee hired by the Department of National Health and Welfare you would have to have two new civil servants appointed by the Department of National Revenue. I think the minister should be persuaded to allow us a supper break while he looks into the points I and other members of the committee have made this afternoon.

Let me pursue this subject a little further by asking one more question. I cannot agree with the minister's suggestion that all those pensioners who have complex income structures are now filing income tax returns. It is possible to have a complex income structure without receiving sufficient income requiring you to file an income tax return. Only those people who have a taxable income after claiming their personal exemptions are required to file an income tax return.
Some senior citizens may have small property holdings which do not return a sufficient net income to be taxable. It seems to me that in fairness we should apply the same laws in arriving at net income in order that our senior citizens may obtain the benefit of supplements. They should be allowed to make the same deductions from their gross income as they are in arriving at net income for the purposes of taxation. Many of these senior citizens are not familiar with deductions and exemptions. Their net incomes may have been worked out over the years by the national revenue department. With all deference to the minister, I cannot accept his suggestion that senior citizens who have complex income structures necessarily file income tax forms.

However, Mr. Chairman, now we are told that if we do not do this we will not have a supper break, or we may have to stay later before Christmas or come back earlier after the new year. This is the type of thing to which I object. We are here on serious business, and the serious business before us right now is trying to get this bill put into the shape in which it should be, in order to meet valid objections that have been raised by responsible members in the house. What surprises me is that the Minister of National Health and Welfare will not yield, when the point has been impressed upon him time and time again, and make the necessary adjustment.
Let me repeat our point. The secrecy of the Income Tax Act is being affected by this intrusion if the bill. All we are asking is that we retain the secrecy of the Income Tax Act and not try to modify it through other bills that may be passed by this house. In order to bring the matter to a head, Mr. Chairman, I propose the following amendment:
That section 17, subsection (3) (a) be modified as follows:
That all the words after the word "purpose" in line 46, page 9, be struck out and the following substituted therefor: "a report as to the accuracy of the information concerning income submitted by the applicant."
Then the section would read as follows:
(3) Notwithstanding any other act or law,
(a) the Minister of National Revenue or any person designated by him for the purpose may, upon the request of the minister furnish to the minister or to any officer or employee in the Department of National Health and Welfare designated by the minister for the purpose, a report as to the accuracy of the information concerning income submitted by the applicant.
I send this amendment up to you, sir. I move it, seconded by the hon. member for Ontario. I suggest that if this wording is not satisfactory to the law officers of the crown, it can be modified so that it will stand up under scrutiny. The intent and purpose as expressed by the minister himself is contained in the suggested amendment. There will be no intrusion on the secrecy of income tax returns. It is not a question of the officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare asking the Department of National Revenue to give them the figures on income tax returns of an applicant; it is the other way around. The

DEBATES	December 19, 1966
Department of National Health and Welfare submits the figures given by the applicant in disclosing his income for the purposes of this act, and the Department of National Revenue, without showing any form of giving any additional information or anything of that nature, or disclosing the secrecy of the information they have at their disposal, simply replies, "the information is accurate" or, "It is inaccurate". I suppose they would have to expand upon the last statement and say, "There is a lack of disclosure of further income". Then, the onus of proof rests on the applicant to show that he has disclosed his full income.
There is no need then for any search of additional questions by the Department of National Health and Welfare of the Department of National Revenue. The income tax return then stays as it is now, not open to any one at all. The Minister of Finance twice, last week and again today, mentioned the fact that under the act of that department they are prohibited-these are the words he used today-from forwarding information to any other department or authority. It is rather interesting that on Friday the Minister of Finance used words similar to that and again today he used those words, just as if he were somehow indirectly attempting to influence the Minister of National Health and Welfare with regard to this section in the bill. I am sure the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue could not agree on this provision because it is opening the door to what has been secret in the past with regard to income tax returns.
I would, therefore, suggest that amendment, sir, or an amendment that can be fixed up by the law officers of the crown so that it will not be misunderstood by anybody. I drafted the amendment hastily here, of course; but I repeat that it shows the intent that the minister himself disclosed this afternoon.

DEBATES	December 19, 1966
mentioned, criminal action could be taken. I make this brief point: the courts of this land are most unwilling that criminal processes should be used to recover civil debts. By putting these words in the bill a heavy club is placed over the heads of the people who might, in all innocence, have been unable to fill out the form correctly.
These people might think they are entitled to benefit when they applied and then, after they had received it, it would turn out that they were not. Ordinarily, under the criminal law, mens rea or criminal intent would be a factor. But this is not so under 21 (1) (c) which deals with a simple failure to return an overpayment. A person might not be in a position to do so. He might have received the money without there being a criminal thought in his head. Yet, he can be brought before a magistrate's court.
I realize the minister may say this is precisely the same procedure as that which now exists in connection with old age security legislation. But I do not believe it is the same. I can see that under old age security legislation if a person fraudulently gives an incorrect age as a means of obtaining benefit to which he is not entitled, that person should be punished. But in the present case the mistakes which arise will, more likely, be errors of judgment. For this reason, I suggest that either 21 (1) (c) be removed from the bill or, if the minister wishes to keep this paragraph, the word "fraudulently" be placed in front of it so that there must be evidence of criminal intent before any action can succeed in the courts.

Mr. Chairman, if the minister gives consideration to this point I think he will make the alteration, because the fact that the section is almost a duplicate of the old section 9(1) indicates that we failed to do our duty when that legislation was before the house.
With respect to the "knowingly", I point out that you cannot knowingly fail to return a cheque just because you do not return it. The "knowingly" cannot refer to the failure to return a cheque or the amount thereof, as required by section 20. No one wants to convict a person for failure to return a cheque or the amount thereof, as required by section 20, unless that is done in a fraudulent manner or with intent. The minister says that of course the department would not prosecute a case unless there were fraud, but the fact remains that the law being what it is, on the face of it a person could be convicted.
For example, let us say I receive a cheque. I place myself in that position, not that I will ever get one under this legislation or indeed under the old age pension legislation at all, but if I got a cheque and did not return it it could have been negligence. It could have been through failure to appreciate the necessity of returning it. Therefore I am sure that if the minister looks into this he will realize that as it stands mere neglect could convict a person under paragraph (c). With respect to paragraph (b), that paragraph reads:
(b) being the payee thereof, negotiates or attempts to negotiate any cheque to which he is not entitled,
There the intent is present because if the payee negotiates or attempts to negotiate any cheque to which he is not entitled the law presumes that that person knows the natural consequence of his act. Paragraph (b) is therefore all right, but under paragraph (c) the failure to return the cheque or the amount thereof should only be made an offence when it is done with a fraudulent purpose. I can see no reason why the minister would not accept the reasonable suggestion made by the hon. member for Halifax.

All these sections, of course, will be difficult to interpret should the legislature of the province of Quebec carry out its intention as evidenced by the speech from the throne. I should like to hear from the minister in this connection. We have been waiting with anticipation and hope that he would be able to explain what on the face of it appears to be unexplainable. Possibly that is the reason that up to the present moment he has shown no avid disposition to place before the committee and the country the views of the government on this very important matter.
When these moneys are paid into the consolidated revenue fund and a province has opted out-I presume that is the proper expression to use-from the federal legislation, what is the government's intention? There must be a decision made in this regard. The government knows now what it is going to do. No doubt it has discussed this matter at length. It evolved the system of opting out. I want to see the govermnent opt in in so far as this legislation is concerned and place the house and the country in full possession of the facts and the view of the government.
The minister has an unusual capacity for explanation. He has shown that in respect of different bills. He has made a thorough study of this matter. The very simple question I place before him arises out of the constitutional issue. Does the government not agree that if any province so decides it may have its own old age pension plan? If that be the interpretation, and I can see no other on the basis of the statute as it now is and on the basis of the section in the B.N.A. Act, then if the legislature of a province decides it is going to have its own system for its own province, old age pensions being within the jurisdiction of the province except in respect of the limitations made by the amendment of some years ago, how is the government going to go about it? Are you going to take the moneys out of this fund which have been collected from the people of nine provinces and hand them over to the tenth province? If two provinces follow this course, are you going to use the moneys collected from the people of eight provinces and hand them to the other two provinces with no strings attached?
You are not going to get this legislation through until you tell us this. We simply want your answer. We will accept it. We know that you will have an ingenious plan in mind. I should like to know how you are going to do it and on what you have determined. The Prime Minister has stated in effect that constitutionally the government is convinced that the
11330	COMMONS DEBATES	December 19, 1966
Old Age Security Act Amendment course it is following is entirely a correct and apt one. However, the government of the province of Quebec, following in the footsteps of its predecessor and also the incitement given by the Prime Minister and members of the government to the opting out concept, has declared its intention to establish its own system. We want to know what you are going to do about it. This is not a matter for next month or next year; it is not being postponed until July 1, 1968. This legislation is to come into effect immediately and, that being so, we are most anxious to know how this abstruse proposition is going to be met by a government noted for its diplomatic approach to problems and its failure to face up to those problems.
I am sure many thousands of people will await with tense interest the explanation of the minister. It is something that will tax the capacity of the government. That is about the only thing which has been left untaxed by this government, and we will get more taxes tonight. How are you going to do this? You collect the money through taxation, and the rumours are that all this government will be able to do will be to increase the income tax of those who have incomes of $6,000 or over. My friend moves his head in a negative manner. What are you going to do about this matter? When you collect the money how are you going to distribute it? You cannot force any province to accept something which constitutionally falls within the ambit of its authority.
I do not wish to detain the minister. It may be that he is not ready to reply and would like to stand this question along with the others until he is able to secure information.

That Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is not intended to be a full-fledged budget statement with the usual details of our finances and of the economic situation. I shall take the opportunity for a brief interim review of our fiscal position and its relation to the economic situation, but my main purpose tonight is to place before the house proposals for financing the guaranteed income supplement for those receiving old age security pensions. We shall be having to pay out about another $280 million a year for this purpose, commencing as soon as possible after January 1st, and I shall propose that we raise additional revenues of about that amount for budget and economic reasons.
In July, at the time of the announcement of the guaranteed income supplement, it was made clear that the government intended to cover the cost by additions to revenue. On September 8th, as the house will recall, I stated:
It was indicated in July that revenue measures would have to be considered to meet the burden of the income guarantee program. I have reached the conclusion that when this program is enacted it will be necessary to increase taxes or to introduce new taxes to meet our total requirements and to prevent the government's own increasing expenditures from having inflationary effects.
December 19, 1966

In the last two completed fiscal years,
1964-	65 and 1965-66, that is, the two years ended 1966, our budgets have been very close to a balance in terms of our public accounts -there have been deficits amounting to only about one half of one per cent of our revenues. Looking at the position from a somewhat different point of view, that is, the overall economic effect of the federal government's receipts and disbursements, what the economists refer to as the national income accounts, there were surpluses of some $300 million in 1964-65 and about $600 million in
1965-	66. These surpluses, in economic terms, have been helpful in pacing our economic expansion and in providing some of the savings required to finance the high level of investment needed for our rapidly growing economy.
Current Year Figures
In the current fiscal year I now forecast that our budgetary revenues before the tax changes I shall propose would be approximately $8,240 million compared with $8,300 million forecast in the budget last March. The reduction is chiefly due to corporate profits turning out to be less than expected, with the taxes thereon correspondingly reduced. In addition of course, the forecasts now reflect the effects of additional income tax abatements granted in favour of the provinces effective January 1st. I expect that our expenditures Will be about $8,580 million compared with $8,450 million forecast in the budget last March. The increases here are spread over a large variety of programs and reflect in considerable part the increased levels of pay and prices. These forecasts of revenues and expenditures would leave us with a budgetary deficit of approximately $340 million compared with the budget forecast of $150 million. Our surplus in terms of the national economic accounts I would forecast at roughly $140 million compared with the budget forecast of $455 million. The refundable tax on cash profits is excluded from both of these figures.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Our net financing requirements for nonbudgetary transactions, before tax changes and excluding transactions in our own debt, I estimate to be $342 million compared with $190 million at the time of the budget, taking into account the refundable tax. Members of the house will recall that in my last budget speech I said that it was not my intention to
The Budget-Mr. Sharp disburse the funds received from the refundable tax but to hold them as an addition to cash balances unless economic circumstances were to change and make it desirable for us to borrow less and ease the pressure on the capital market. This is still my intention. The possibility cannot be excluded of course, that our requirements will make it necessary for the government to borrow extra funds in the market before the end of the fiscal year.
Prospects for 1967-68
I do not propose at this time to forecast the budget for the next fiscal year. That will be done in the spring as usual. Our expenditure programs are still being worked out by the Treasury Board. It is still too early to forecast the economic position with enough accuracy and confidence to estimate our revenues. It is already evident, however, that our expenditures will continue to rise next year quite apart from the guaranteed income supplement. We have already taken on two major commitments in increased equalization payments to the provinces and substantially increased assistance for higher education. We have many large and important programs which are expanding, such as those for scientific research and development, and those for foreign aid. These are worthy projects supported strongly in this house and by the public. Having said this, I want to repeat what I said in this house on September 8th and on other occasions, that we must moderate the rate of increase in new public expenditures. Neither the capacity nor the willingness of Canadians to pay higher taxes should be taken for granted.
On the revenue side the situation in the next year is complicated by our relations and arrangements with the provinces. Already we have undertaken to recommend to parliament
a further abatement of our income taxes____
personal and corporate-next year in order to make more room for the provinces to increase such taxes to meet the rapidly rising costs of higher education including technical education. The income tax bill, which I plan to introduce before the recess to implement the portions of the March budget resolutions not dealt with in the bill passed in July, will contain clauses to provide for these abatements. In view of the discussion in the committee last friday, I might also mention at this time that we had put in this bill a specific provision exempting from tax social assistance payments based on needs or means, and made under either federal or provincial legislation.

December 19. 196S
The Budget-Mr. Sharp Economic Situation
When I reviewed the economic situation in September, I thought that it might be necessary to increase our revenues in order to counteract the increase in some of our other expenditures this year, and to make possible some relaxation in monetary restraint. Developments in the past three months, however, suggest to me that the undesirable acceleration of the demands upon our economy has moderated. There has been some economic readjustment taking place following the excessive rates of expansion that occurred earlier this year. The effects of a large number of strikes have also been appearing in the statistics. My judgment is that the economic expansion now taking place is more in line with the capability of our economy to grow steadily without inflation. While prices and wages are increasing at rates that are still excessive, I now believe we can expect some moderation in the trend of wage increases and further restraint in pricing policies. Our current position is one of delicate balance and we want to ensure that our economic policies do not contribute either to a serious decline in 1967 or to a re-emergence of strong inflationary pressures as we attempt to adjust to a sustained rate of economic growth.
The Canadian economic outlook for 1967 cannot be fully assessed as yet. We do not yet know enough of the capital spending plans of business or of provinces and municipalities. I believe, however, the rate of increase in such capital expenditures will be less than in the past two years, and should be a closer match to our growing capacity. Moreover, our exports, and our general business behaviour, are much influenced by the economic situation in the United States and that is unusually difficult to foresee this December. Within a few weeks we will know much more of United States policy in regard to defence expenditures and the fiscal measures likely to be proposed to deal with them. We will be in a much better position in several months to appraise our outlook and take promptly such action as may be necessary. Should some relaxation of restraint be needed there will be no difficulty in moving quickly in either the monetary or fiscal field or both. For example, the government will not hesitate to bring before parliament at short notice a measure to end the collection of the refundable tax on business profits or even to make reductions in taxes if that is necessary to achieve a proper fiscal policy for economic reasons. I believe,

and in this my views are shared by the governor of the Bank of Canada, that the appropriate mix of policies in such circumstances would be one which permitted some easing of the credit situation.
On the other hand, in 1967 we cannot be expected to permit a degree of expansion of the total demands on the economy that would encourage or endorse further increases in wages and prices at the rates that have been occuring during 1966. If some moderation in demands with inflationary consequences does not occur we may well find it necessary to impose sufficient fiscal restraint upon the economy as a whole to check them. At this time, I am very happy to say, it does not appear such further action will be necessary, and I certainly hope it will not be.
General Policy
Consequently, I am not proposing tonight any general changes in taxation for the purpose either of stimulating or of applying further restraints to the economy. The measures proposed are intended only to counterbalance, financially and economically, the expenditures on the guaranteed income supplement with a small margin to allow for the fact that the payments we make to the old age pensioners are sure to be spent while some of the revenues we get will come out of savings. Given our present economic and budgetary situation, I believe this neutral action to be about right.
To raise all the revenues that are required by all governments in Canada-about $18 billion a year currently-requires a large variety of taxes and charges. We can count on a growth in these revenues as our economy grows and prospers but the rate of real growth in the economy is limited by the growth in our labour force and the improvement in its use and productivity. It is all too easy to anticipate the growth in our revenues and to commit ourselves to spending programs that outrun it. The consequence of over-running it, which those who elect us and make demands on us must face, is that we must raise by increased taxes for public purposes or for redistribution of income an increasing fraction of our total national product. It is because we are in that position that tonight we are asking the Canadian public to accept increased taxes in order that we may distribute more to our old age pensioners with low incomes.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Old Age Security Fund
I turn now to the tax measures I am proposing-two increases in existing taxes. The first
December 19, 1966	COMMONS
is an increase in one of the taxes under the Old Age Security Act, which will increase the revenues of the old age security fund. Let me first explain the situation of that fund and the policy I propose in regard to it.
When the Old Age Security Act was passed late in 1951 it set up this fund to which were to be credited the revenues from certain specified taxes levied under that act, and which were regarded at the time as essentially contributions for the financing of the pensions authorized by the act. While individual pensions were not related to the taxes or contributions paid by the pensioner, it was felt the aggregate pensions should be related to the revenues of the fund. This was intended to be a means of ensuring the proper financing of the pensions and of ensuring a sense of responsibility in determining from time to time how much the pensions ought to be. The Minister of Finance is required to review an-
The Budget-Mr. Sharp nually the state of the fund and to recommend measures to increase the revenues of the fund if it appears the revenues for the ensuing year will not be sufficient to meet the charges on the fund without further loans from the consolidated revenue fund.
I would ask permission of the house to insert here in Hansard, for the convenience of hon. members, a table showing for each fiscal year since the act was passed the pension payments made from the fund, the revenues credited to it for each of the three taxes levied under the act, and finally the deficit or surplus for the year, with footnotes indicating how these deficits were dealt with.
