The Budget-Mr. Sharp amounts to much the same except for accounting purposes. Hon. Donald Fleming, in his budget of April, 1959, concerned over these increasing deficits taken in conjunction with the recent increases in pension rates, increased the rates of all three old age security taxes from 2 per cent to 3 per cent, which brought about a rough balance in the fund for the next three years. Increasing deficits then occurred, accelerated by the increase in pensions early in 1962. They were financed by temporary loans from the consolidated revenue fund. When the rate of the pension was increased to the present level in the autumn of 1963 the rate of contribution from the tax on personal incomes was raised from 3 per cent to 4 per cent effective January, 1964. This, together with the removal of exemptions from the sales tax and the effects on revenues of increasing incomes and sales, brought in sufficient revenue to produce surpluses in the fund during the past two fiscal years, and this year as well. These have resulted in the repayment of the temporary loans made to the fund in the preceding two years and the accumulation of a credit balance of $217 million at the end of the last fiscal year, and of $353 million at the end of October. This surplus is much less, it will be noted, than the total deficits in the fund in the 1950's that were not carried forward but written off. Over the whole period of the fund up to this October, the expenditures have exceeded the revenues by $238 million.
Parliament has recently imposed large additional future burdens on the fund by providing that the age at which payment of pensions will commence will be reduced year by year starting in January, 1966 until it reaches age 65 in January, 1970. Even after taking account of the growing revenues of the fund, the increasing pensions would exceed the annual revenues in the fiscal year 1970-71, when the full effects of the age reduction are first felt. Addition of the guaranteed income supplement, however, would immediately bring the pensions in the next fiscal year 1967-68 above the revenues anticipated from the present taxes, and this annual deficit would grow rapidly. It would use up the accounting surplus in the fund by mid-1969 and produce an annual deficit of nearly $400 million in the fund by the time the age reduction already in the law takes full effect.
Such is the situation in terms of this particular account. When we consider the economic and financial effects of old age security payments, however, we must look not to the position in a single account but to total cash
[Mr. Sharp.l
flows. In introducing the guaranteed income supplement we are adding $280 million a year to our cash outflow, and this must somehow be matched by increased cash revenues if we are to avoid increasing our cash deficit with all its financial and economic consequences. The accumulated surplus of the old age security account is not held in a separate cash balance. The cash received and credited to this account is and always has been pooled in the consolidated revenue fund into which parliament requires all revenues to be paid and from which the payments authorized by parliament are made. If parliament increases the payments out of this consolidated revenue fund, it must replenish the fund with revenues, or the government has to borrow more to finance the deficit. Given the present and prospective economic situation I do not think that we should finance this large increased cash outflow by increased borrowing. If the economic situation should develop in a way that makes it desirable to reduce our cash inflow from taxes, and borrow more, we can quickly take action to do this. But we should not use the possibility of such a contingency as an excuse for taking the soft option and dodging a difficult issue.
Old Age Security Tax On Income
I am proposing therefore that we act to meet our immediate cash requirements and also to provide properly in our accounts for the burdens which parliament has imposed and is now imposing on the old age security fund during the next four years while the age reduction program is coming fully into effect. The first measure I recommend to the house, therefore, is that we raise the maximum amount payable by an individual on the 4 per cent tax on personal income under the Old Age Security Act, from $120 per year, as it has been for the past three years, to $240 per year. This would yield about $135 million a year at current income levels. It would be effective from January 1st but since deduction at the source cannot start immediately, relatively little will appear in this fiscal year's accounts. The forecast effects of this change on the future years' accounts of the old age security fund are shown in a table which I would ask permission to place in Hansard at this point for the assistance of hon. members.

Addition to General Revenues
The second tax change I am recommending is intended to add to our general revenues to provide the remaining cash required to pay the guaranteed income supplement.
The choice of the tax to increase for this purpose is a difficult one. Normally one would look to our regular personal income tax because, being progressive, it is one of our fairest taxes. However, we share this tax field with the provinces. We have emphasized to them in recent months that they have access to this field of taxation just as we do and must share responsibility for its use. We are proposing, as I have said, to abate our income tax for 1967 to make it easier for the provinces to raise theirs in order to help finance the rapidly growing burden of higher education. We will want to discuss with the provinces in the coming year or two various ideas proposed to reform the income tax so that we may achieve as much harmony as possible in our use of this most important tax field.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
In these circumstances and having in mind the impending major overhaul of our tax system which we will undertake in the light of the report of the Royal Commission on Taxation, I have come to the conclusion that we should not use the personal income tax to 
raise the additional funds we need now. We must, at this time, as the provinces frequently have to do, rely upon other taxes to meet our increasing burdens.
In making the choice of taxes we must also keep in mind that the corporate income tax in Canada cannot get seriously out of line with that in the United States without endangering our competitive position. Already our competitive position is being weakened by recent increases in costs.

The company has failed dismally, causing untold hardship to countless citizens who had every reason to suppose their life earnings were safe. Many hundreds are destitute. This sort of thing has gone far enough. How many more financial calamities will there be before this government acts?
Ask Robarts.

There seems to be a difference of opinion as to the extent of federal and provincial jurisdiction in certain fields of finance. To a degree I think these differences arise because of the lack of a proper
December 19, 1966

definition of banking. During recent meetings of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs almost all witnesses have indicated their belief that there should be an alternative to the present definition which simply says that a bank is "a bank to which this Act applies". Then a list of banks is given in a schedule. I suggest that the government should at least take action to the extent of asking the Supreme Court of Canada for a decision; otherwise we could go on forever suffering confusion. I know there is no law which prevents any individual from accepting money and paying interest thereon, but when corporations set themselves up in the business of taking loans, then surely protection should be afforded to persons lending money to such corporations.
The minister told us he acted in the only way open to him; he could not have done other than he did. I say he was wrong. Whether or not Mr. Gruber expected the Minister of Finance to pass on his warnings to the Ontario authorities is beside the point. I say the minister should have done so. It was his duty. The fate of hundreds and hundreds of depositors was at stake. The minister says it was none of his business. I say it was. Surely he owed something to those people all over Canada who today are suffering from this mess.
The minister has not only been negligent; he has done a great deal of damage to the reputation of sound and reputable Canadian insurance companies. On December 12 he made statements both inside and outside the house which could have implied that only British and foreign companies were dependable and safe. The inference was that Canadian companies do not have any securities deposited with the Department of Finance in Ottawa. In this connection I would refer to a letter which I have received from the managing director of a Canadian insurance company. He writes:
As you probably know, a good deal of damage to the reputation of Canadian insurance companies has been done, principally because of the impression created that the Canadian companies do not have any deposits at all in Ottawa.

The managing director goes on to say:
As one of the smaller Canadian companies we have deposits with the minister in excess of $400,000 and of course comply fully with the requirements of the department. The letter goes on to point out that the minister's somewhat half-hearted retraction received considerably less publicity than his original damaging statement. The damage has been done, the writer states. The minister should make a stronger retraction. I suggest this is an example of the ineptitude with which the minister has been handling this whole affair, offering nothing but alibis.

I have no objection. It is the Perth Mutual Fire Insurance Company of Stratford. The minister even procrastinated about the one small step he has taken in the hope that it might eventually provide some protection. His deposit insurance legislation is not obligatory on institutions other than the chartered banks, so I understand, and the chartered banks do not need it. The most important aspect of this matter, however, is that we have not seen the legislation. It has been promised for months and months, and when asked about it the minister simply says, "soon". This ridiculous situation has existed continually since the finance committee has been meeting to study amendments to the Bank Act. We have expert witnesses appearing before us; yet we can only ask hypothetical questions because the legislation is not available to us. It is an unbelievable situation.
I would also make a strong complaint about the lack of action on the part of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) in the deplorable bankruptcy of Prudential Finance. When the officials of his department heard allegations of possible fraud, why did his income tax inspectors not make an investigation for income tax purposes? He would have been justified in taking such action. It is easy to conclude what would have been the result if he had taken this step. The minister should not suggest it would be improper to take this

The Budget-Mr. Monteith action. We know his inspectors often make investigations of taxpayers on less evidence than was available in this case.
Income tax inspectors often take action after receiving anonymous tips. Maybe these are provided to the department out of pique, jealousy, or for some other reason. Sometimes, I understand, the department even pays rewards for such information. Here we have a case where a definite warning has been ignored. Had the minister acted promptly something, at least, might have been saved.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Now let us look at tonight's budget. In a way it too is in the pattern of this government's failure to look at Canada and the practical needs of our people. Mr. Speaker, I suggest th!s budget presented to us tonight should never have been delivered. There is no need for it. True, the minister said last September 8 he would present a budget this autumn. But that was last September. He knows the economic situation in Canada is standing still, if not in a recession, and I suggest the minister is not doing anything to improve the situation.
If any second budget is necessary then it should only be because of a real crisis. I claim there is not that crisis to bring on this effort of the minister's tonight, even though there has been plenty of poor planning. All this is going to do is make it more difficult for the average person to get by in his or her day-today existence.
Hear, hear.

We have faced, are facing, and will in the future face frightening increases in the cost of living. Is it really any wonder that we have been having demands for larger pay increases? The housewife goes marketing and she finds food, clothing, whatever it may be, continuing to rise in price and at a rapid rate. She goes home and tells her husband and naturally he is unhappy and anxious to demand higher pay, but the Pearson formula of wage increases has set standards which can have only one outcome. The resultant increased costs have not even been felt yet, and now the minister takes another slice off the husband's take-home pay.
It is interesting to compare some of the prices the housewife in Canada pays compared with those the housewife pays in the United States. I have here a comparison list of food prices in Canada and the United States. I have taken prices from advertisements in the Ottawa Journal of December 14, and American food prices from advertisements in

the Washington Post of December 12, just two days previous.
In Canada sirloin steaks were advertised at 97 cents a pound; in Washington they were advertised at 87 cents a pound. Bacon in Ottawa was advertised at 89 cents a pound and in Washington at 65 cents a pound. Chicken breasts were advertised in Ottawa at 65 cents a pound and at 45 cents a pound in Washington.
What size?

Frozen french fries were advertised at 59 cents for two pounds in Ottawa and at 29 cents for two pounds in Washington. Hon. members opposite may think this is funny, but the average Canadian housewife does not think it funny when she goes to the supermarkets.
Hear, hear.

I give one more example. Picnic ham was advertised at 49 cents a pound in Ottawa and at 37 cents a pound in Washington. These are just five items from the list. The housewife in Washington is paying considerably less for food than the housewife at the local supermarket in Canada.
And the salaries are better in the United States.

Yes, the salaries are better. There are many things that the minister could have done to bolster our economy at this time when it is so direly in need of bolstering. He could have accelerated the withdrawal of the sales tax on building supplies and materials. This would have encouraged home construction, so badly needed. Tonight the minister apparently thought he was doing quite a thing when he refused to add the extra 1 per cent sales tax on to building materials, but he has left the tax on construction materials. If he really wanted to do something to encourage the Canadian economy I repeat that he could have accelerated withdrawal of the 11 per cent sales tax on building supplies.
He could have rescinded the 5 per cent forced savings tax on certain corporations. This would assist in expanding production to meet the demand and help combat inflation. He could have abolished the amendments to the Income Tax Act introduced by his predecessor, which were supposed to encourage minority Canadian ownership in foreign controlled companies. It has not worked. The minister knows it, and abolishing it might

have stopped some repatriation of funds to the United States.
But the best thing of all that he could have done would have been to admit his error and not brought down a budget until next spring.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, all predictions seem to be that tight money is here to stay for some years. When a company like Imperial Oil issues 20-year debentures at 6f per cent, non-callable for 12 years, it is easily seen what it thinks of the money market. These high interest rates can only add to the cost of production and the high cost of living. Mr. Speaker, we are being squeezed out of the markets of the world by the restrictive and negative approach that the government has been taking.
Why does not the government itself practice some economy and set a pattern for others, particularly other governments? Surely this would be the first step in any sensible approach. Mr. Speaker, I claim the government is guilty of gross fiscal mismanagement.
Hear, hear.
Spending money like a drunken sailor.

Let us look for a moment at Canada's economic condition and ask ourselves what will be the effect of more taxation. Look at housing. In the third quarter of this year house construction dropped by 25 per cent, from 49,551 units to 37,145 units. Housing construction is in a serious position, so what does the minister do? Tax more.
Look at the stock market. There is actually a net outflow of funds to the United States because American equity stocks now look so attractive by comparison with prospects here. This is a dreadful commentary on the state of Canada on the eve of its centennial. In the first eight months of 1966 we had a net outflow of $308 million compared with $174 million in the same period of 1965 and only $53 million in the same period of 1964. So we tax more.
We should be encouraging Canadians to invest in their own country. This is not the time to raise taxes in Canada. There are many signs that while the cost of living continues to rise, there is a tapering off or a slowdown ahead in economic activity. This is happening both in Canada and in the United States.
Car production and steel production have declined in the United States. New car sales
The Budget-Mr. Monteith are down. A particularly volatile item is the level of debt in the United States. The average United States consumer is now paying out 22 per cent of his income to pay off debt, compared with 19 per cent only six years ago. The consumer, so important in maintaining a boom, is in no position to increase his spending in that country.
Similarly, Mr. Speaker, in Canada consumer credit is high. Total consumer credit now stands at over $7,000 million, compared with only $4,000 million just six years ago. The cash loans of consumer loan companies now are double the level of just six years ago. The personal loans of chartered banks are some $2,370 million, nearly double the level of just over two years ago.
Our people are so in debt and our financial institutions are so lent out that there is a real danger that demand cannot be sustained in the consumer sector of the economy. Yet this is the time the government adds to the burden by increasing taxes. President Johnson has held off any tax increase in the United States; yet our government goes ahead in its stubborn way. I wonder whether the Minister of Finance really does know the state of the Canadian economy. Mr. Speaker, I should like to reiterate that this party is against the means test. Our party's position is firmly against the means test in old age security. Now we have added the other side-a mean tax. We have proposed a $100 a month pension to all pensioners at an estimated additional cost of $100 million.
We are against the government's new gimmick. I should like to point out why. It reintroduces the means test which has been abolished since 1951. The minister has said that out-of-country benefits will not be paid because they are too hard to investigate. Are we going to bring back the regime of the prying eye? We are against it because it does nothing for the pensioners who are faced with cost of living increases, and again tonight there is going to be an increased cost of living to the pensioners. The $75 a month to the pensioners, given later in 1963, is worth a lot less today. The consumer price index has jumped nearly 12 points since the last pension increase. Today's pension of $75 is worth less than $66 in real terms. Yet nothing is being done to improve the lot of these Canadians.
Another one per cent has been added to the sales tax.

Yes, another 1 per cent has been added to the sales tax tonight which will have to be met by those in the middle and high income groups. I am not pleading the case for those in the high income brackets. I

am thinking of those in the low income brackets. I should like to ask the Minister of Finance what is the size of the old age security fund. I believe he gave us that information this evening. I think it was $353 million as at the end of October. What right is there to overtax the Canadian people and hold out on our old age pensioners? Is the government by any chance holding off until the eve of another election?
I realize that the cost of social welfare has to be met, but I understand that the legislation concerning the Canada Assistance Plan has not yet been proclaimed and that no payments are to be made under the old age security amendments which are now before us until at least next March or April. But then, this is Christmas. As Dickens said of Scrooge:
And it was always said of him that he knew how to keep Christmas well, if any man alive possessed the knowledge.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, why bring in this tax now and further dampen down the economy? The date of the next regular budget would have been plenty early enough. Psychologically this is not the time to increase any taxes. To me this budget seems to be an exercise in nonsense. It is not needed and will only put a further brake on our economy and again increase the cost of living as do all taxes.
This budget obviously does not meet the needs of Canadians today. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard):
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
The government give consideration to meeting the proposed selective means test payments for old age pensioners by drawing on the surplus now in the old age security fund, before any increase be made in the oppressive burden of general taxation whose effects at this time will intensify rather than alleviate the hardships being experienced by Canadians generally, whose living standards are being seriously reduced by inflation and by the steadily rising cost of living.

SHIPPING-USE OF RUSSIAN ICEBREAKER IN ST. LAWRENCE RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last December 13, I put the following question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill):
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Transport whether it is true that the Russian government recently announced that a Russian icebreaker would be assigned to the St. Lawrence river next winter in order to make winter shipping easier for Russian ships on that river?
I was expecting a serious answer from the minister as to whether that was true or not. But all he said was that he was not a spokesman for the Russian government. Well, I think that if the Russian government had to choose a spokesman, it would not select him.
Mr. Speaker, my question was based on an article published not on the news page but as an editorial of the Toronto Telegram on December 9, 1966. This is what it said, and I quote:

Moscow also recently announced that a Soviet icebreaker would be assigned to the St. Lawrence river this winter to ease the way for the vessels of the Soviet merchant fleet. Surely Canada won't permit this. If we are to have a winter route, we should maintain it ourselves.

Mr. Speaker, this is quite clear and written not by a news reporter but by an editor. All this was taken from a notice published by the Minister of Transport in number 48 of a weekly publication which is not even published in French in spite of the statements of the hon. minister concerning bilingualism in Canada. The December 2, 1966 edition-which is fairly recent-of this publication, Notice to Mariners, contained notice No. 1023, entitled:

The St. Lawrence river-Quebec harbour to Montreal harbour-assistance of icebreakers.
Commercial shipping using the St. Lawrence river ship channel between Montreal and Quebec is hereby warned that floating aids to navigation cannot be depended upon after November 30 owing to possible ice conditions.
December 19, 1966

Commercial shipping is also warned that icebreaker assistance to ships will not be available in this area. A small force of icebreakers will be working there but this will be for the sole purpose of preventing flooding.

Mr. Speaker, the notice is very clear, icebreakers will not be there to give assistance to winter shipping but for the sole purpose of preventing flooding.
To have 11 icebreakers and not allow them to open the St. Lawrence to winter navigation and moreover to force the Russians to attend to this matter is something ridiculous and stupid.
I have here an editorial from La Presse of Saturday December 10, 1966, signed by Mr. Roger Champoux, bearing the title: "Running with the hare and hunting with the hounds".
The Gllles G rcgoire incident, which has been for 20 hours the subject of current events, has permitted the minister to give those who are interested in winter navigation on the St. Lawrence, the most ambiguous answer possible.
Closely questioned by Mr. Gregoire, the minister, who means to be wise, (and he is so), answered the following: "I do not propose to take extraordinary steps to accelerate such navigation no more than I propose to take any steps to impede it". The hounds ... are Halifax; the hare . . . is Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, another newspaper that can surely not be branded as separatist, the Montreal Gazette, said in its editorial on December 10, 1966:

The government is making a mistake in limiting the role of its icebreakers in keeping the St. Lawrence channel open in winter, up to Montreal. [DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
It is easy to understand that the government is sensitive about feelings in the maritimes. If too much is done to keep the St. Lawrence open in winter, if too much is done to make Montreal a winter port, complaints from the maritime ports will come thick and fast.
But in its policy the government is really trying to turn the clock back or, at least, is hesitant about helping it forward.

That is, Mr. Speaker, the government's policy. In that respect, the Estates General of French Canada submitted a working paper at their last meeting and here is their conclusion.
We conclude that it is unacceptable that, to satisfy the ports of St. John and Halifax, the government should impede directly or indirectly the development of winter navigation on the St. Lawrence and the Saguenay rivers, experience having shown that winter navigation is possible and economic for the big ports on the Saguenay and the St. Lawrence up to Montreal inclusive and that it is more economical for shipping to go as far as possible inland.

Those owners of ships who want to take the risks of plying these waters in winter are not impeded in any way. If they get into any kind of distress, then, as with any other ship, we do our best to meet their problems. It would cost many, many millions of dollars-

Mr. Speaker, at this time I want to put forth two or three vital arguments to explain why it is necessary to get improvements under way on the Pembroke waterfront next year. The present wharf was built after the first world war and consists of wooden piles which support a relieving platform of wooden material. The platform in turn supports a concrete cap and earth fill. When the Des Joachims hydro dam was built, the water level of the Ottawa river in front of this wharf changed considerably and the water level was lowered. As a result portions of the wooden piles and the relieving platform were exposed to the air and serious rotting set in. As the wooden supporting timbers rot, the earth fill on top drops into the water and much of this fill is carried away by the current. In past years large quantities of fill have been placed in the holes that have occurred, but in its present state the wharf has become a menace to the public. Signs stating "This wharf is in disrepair'' have been erected and flex-beams now enclose the whole wharf area. These were put in about three years ago.
At the present time there is a great danger of children being trapped underneath the relieving platform, and several near fatalities have been narrowly averted. The plain truth of the matter is that during the last 40 years very little maintenance work has been done on the wharf and it no longer provides any service. In fact, it has become a detriment to the public.

Therefore my first argument is based on the need for safety by removing this danger. It is now proposed to cut or remove the piles and relieving platform and drop the concrete cap, which would form a shore protection along the north and west end faces, rather than reconstructing both these sections as wharves. A new timber crib wharf, about 200 feet long, should be constructed along the east side, which is generally protected from winds, rather than constructing the north and west faces as wharves. A small breakwater, about 40 feet long, would also be required at the northeast corner to give protection from the prevailing northwest winds.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
The cost of this proposal would not be greater than that of the original proposal advanced by the town about two years ago. In my opinion this is a much better scheme in that the total cost is not more than the original one and furthermore it would develop a small bay at the mouth of the Muskrat river where the town has already placed a large amount of fill to raise a swamp area to be made useful for a small boat harbour.
A fire destroyed the many boathouses in front of the government wharf several years ago and no suitable area has been developed since that time to accommodate the hundreds of boats in the area. I use the term "hundreds of boats" because I have made a check with the customs office in the town of Pembroke and have learned that there are 3,131 small boats registered for that area. This points out the great need for launching facilities on the Ottawa river. In addition, we depend a lot on the tourist trade during the summer months and want to promote this industry inasmuch as Renfrew country in general is so suitable and so attractive.
A launching ramp was placed on the shore of the bay at the west end of the present wharf but there are two major problems with this location. The bay itself has to be dredged now and will have to be dredged from time to time in the future because silt is constantly drifting into it and settling there. Second, in order to launch a boat in that location one must block a road with his car and trailer. The road serves as an exit and entrance to the adjoining municipal park. There is also no place to park cars and trailers satisfactorily. For this reason it has been proposed to move the location of this single boat ramp and put in a double launching ramp at the head of the bay at the mouth of the Muskrat River. The town would be quite willing to deed a right of

I know how much this new development will mean to the safety of youth and to the large percentage of the 3,131 boat owners in the area who would make use of the new facilities. The total amount of money that has been spent on such projects as tourist wharves and launching ramps has been very small over the past years and I would like to recommend that this small amount be increased because it helps to provide good recreation for Canadians.
